title: The One Where Eddie Wont Go

jokes.text: What are you doing here? / Watching you sleep.
jokes.setup: Chandler wakes up startled to find his roommate Eddie in his room in the dark
jokes.punchline: Eddie casually admits he's been watching Chandler sleep, delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — four words deliver a deeply unsettling and funny answer. Eddie's deadpan sincerity transforms a creepy premise into comedy gold. The character specificity is high; this only works because Eddie is established as unhinged. The cold open delivery and audience's gasp-laugh reaction make this one of the episode's strongest moments.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What are you doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: I was just watching you sleep.

jokes.text: It makes me feel, um, peaceful.
jokes.setup: Chandler demands to know WHY Eddie is watching him sleep
jokes.punchline: Eddie gives a serene, self-satisfied answer as if it's perfectly reasonable
jokes.explanation: The 'um' pause before 'peaceful' is crucial — it signals Eddie is genuinely searching for the right word, not performing. His total lack of self-awareness escalates the creepiness-to-comedy ratio. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: Well, I like to watch people sleep. It's peaceful. It's like they're not annoying you for once.

jokes.text: Hannibal Lecter? Better roommate than you.
jokes.setup: Chandler tries to explain why Eddie's sleep-watching behavior is unacceptable
jokes.punchline: Chandler invokes a cannibalistic serial killer as a preferable alternative roommate
jokes.explanation: Sharp economy — the two-fragment structure (name-drop, verdict) is punchy and Chandler-specific. The Hannibal Lecter reference was fresher in 1996 given Silence of the Lambs' recent cultural dominance. Solid Chandler wit.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Eddie is such a bad roommate, I'd rather live with Hannibal Lecter. At least he'd have the decency to eat me instead of driving me crazy with his weird habits.

jokes.text: Last night you went and got some water... and I was nice enough to hide behind the door.
jokes.setup: Eddie defends himself, saying Chandler only sees him when he's awake
jokes.punchline: Eddie reveals he's ALSO been hiding in the apartment during the night — and frames it as a kindness
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first truly exceptional joke. The escalation is perfectly structured: we thought Eddie just watched Chandler sleep, but now we learn he's been HIDING during the night too — and he presents this as a favor. 'I was nice enough to hide behind the door' reframes stalker behavior as generosity, which is a genuinely original comedic inversion. The self-congratulatory delivery makes it devastating. Strong candidate for standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: I haven't been watching you. I've just been here every night, hiding better.

jokes.text: I want to hear it from your lips. / Where'd you hear it before?
jokes.setup: Eddie demands verbal confirmation that Chandler wants him out, saying 'I want to hear it from your lips'
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately implies Eddie has been lip-reading him while he sleeps
jokes.explanation: Clever callback that implies Eddie has been watching Chandler's lips while he sleeps and possibly lip-reading. Maximum economy in the comeback. The implication is funnier than anything explicit could be.

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: I'm nice enough to hide. I don't want to bother you.

jokes.text: Finally got that time machine working, huh?
jokes.setup: Joey walks in wearing an obviously dated or outlandish hat
jokes.punchline: Chandler implies the hat is so out of fashion it must have come from the past via time machine
jokes.explanation: Solid Chandler fashion-burn. The time machine framing is more creative than a straight 'that's ugly' insult. Works well as quick banter.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Where did you hear that? On the radio? Did it come to you in a dream?

jokes.text: 'You know what I don't have?' / A mirror?
jokes.setup: Joey sets up that he saw the hat being sold and thought 'You know what I don't have?'
jokes.punchline: Monica cuts in with 'A mirror?' before he can finish — implying he can't see how bad he looks
jokes.explanation: The interruption structure is well-timed; cutting off Joey mid-setup to deliver the punchline before him is a clean comedic technique. Monica getting the burn in before Chandler is a nice character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Did you just travel here from 1987? Because that outfit is a time machine.

jokes.text: Fine, make fun. I think it's jaunty.
jokes.setup: Joey is being mocked for his ridiculous hat
jokes.punchline: Joey's defense is the word 'jaunty' — clearly a word he just learned and is using to compensate
jokes.explanation: Works because 'jaunty' is such a specific, slightly pompous word choice for Joey, whose vocabulary is usually basic. Sets up the word-of-the-day toilet paper reveal nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What don't I have?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Self-awareness.

jokes.text: Cachet? Jaunty? Chandler gave me word-of-the-day toilet paper.
jokes.setup: Joey has been using surprisingly sophisticated vocabulary words ('cachet,' 'jaunty')
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals his vocabulary source: word-of-the-day toilet paper, which also explains why he's using the words in order
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best constructed joke. It retroactively recontextualizes TWO earlier moments ('jaunty' and 'cachet') in a single payoff — we realize Joey has been using the words sequentially as he learned them. The specificity of 'word-of-the-day TOILET PAPER' is perfect character comedy: only Chandler would give this as a gift, and only Joey would use it as his primary vocabulary source. The joke rewards attentive viewers and would land even harder on rewatch. Exceptional structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I've been feeling quite perspicacious lately, you know? My vocabulary has become rather magnanimous.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Perspicacious? Magnanimous? Who are you and what have you done with Joey?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, right? I've been expanding my lexicon. I'm a very erudite guy now.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey, where are you getting all these words from?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, this fancy toilet paper I bought. It's got a word of the day on every sheet.

jokes.text: It's about how women need to become more empowered. And, oh! But there's wind. And the wind can make us goddesses.
jokes.setup: Rachel enthusiastically describes a self-help book
jokes.punchline: The description devolves into increasingly absurd New Age wind metaphysics delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Functional satire of 90s self-help culture. The enthusiasm Rachel brings makes it work, but the joke is essentially just 'self-help books are silly' without much specific twist.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: See, the book says that people steal your wind, you know? Like, they take your power away. And so you have to, like, protect your wind at all times.

jokes.text: Men just take our wind? / Uh-huh. All the time. Because they are the lightning-bearers.
jokes.setup: Ross repeats back the wind metaphor with barely concealed disbelief
jokes.punchline: Rachel doubles down and adds 'lightning-bearers' as if this clarifies everything
jokes.explanation: Ross's incredulous repetition is a reliable comedic structure, and 'lightning-bearers' as an escalation of the absurdity works. The straight-man/true-believer dynamic is well-deployed here.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know, I think the 'Wind-Keeper' book is actually a feminist metaphor. See, the wind represents the liberation of the female spirit, breaking free from societal constraints — much like in Tolkien's work where the elves represent an idealized, ethereal femininity.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, it's a children's book about a magical wind keeper.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Exactly! And that's what makes it so profound!

jokes.text: That sounds kind of cool. It's like The Hobbit.
jokes.setup: Rachel explains the mystical wind/lightning-bearer mythology from her self-help book
jokes.punchline: Ross, being a nerdy academic, immediately relates it to fantasy literature
jokes.explanation: Excellent character integration — only Ross would respond to a feminist empowerment book by comparing it to Tolkien. The non-sequitur nature and his genuine enthusiasm make it funnier than a dismissive comment would be. Rachel's immediate 'It is nothing like The Hobbit' is the perfectly calibrated straight-man response.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's like when you're trying to fit a square peg in a round hole.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, that is not helping your case.

jokes.text: 'Hello. Who wants one of my phallic-shaped man-cakes?'
jokes.setup: Monica/Rachel are discussing the book's theory about men draining women's power, when a male character offers crullers
jokes.punchline: Rachel/Monica interprets the innocent cruller offering as a literal manifestation of masculine power-taking, performing an exaggerated male voice
jokes.explanation: The absurdist leap from 'cruller' to 'phallic man-cake' is the payoff, and the character performing an exaggerated male voice adds physical comedy. 'Phallic-shaped man-cakes' is a memorably ridiculous phrase. Gets a solid laugh but doesn't rise above the material.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: Can I interest you in a croissant? Or perhaps a Danish?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, well that would be lovely, thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know, in my book 'How to Spot a Pervert in the Workplace,' Chapter 3 is all about this exact scenario.

jokes.text: Joey, look at me. Look at me! Do I have lipstick on my teeth?
jokes.setup: Joey asks his agent Estelle if she's mad at him for getting fired — a serious emotional question
jokes.punchline: Estelle completely ignores the emotional weight and pivots to asking about her lipstick mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: Classic Estelle — her complete self-absorption is perfectly captured in this pivot. The dramatic 'Look at me! Look at me!' builds expectation of a serious moment, which makes the lipstick deflation funnier. Strong character integration for a recurring character.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Are you mad at me?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.line: Mad? No, I'm not mad. But look at me.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.line: Do I look mad to you?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No...

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.line: That's because I just had my Botox refreshed.

jokes.text: Estelle gets Joey an audition for 'Another World' — as 'Cab Driver Number 2'
jokes.setup: Estelle says she already got Joey a new audition, implying good news
jokes.punchline: 'Cab Driver Number 2' — a humiliatingly minor role for someone who was a series regular
jokes.explanation: The specific credit 'Cab Driver Number 2' (not even Number 1) is a nice detail that shows the writers knew how to calibrate humiliation. Functional but predictable fall-from-grace comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.line: Listen, if you want to make it in this business with a dog act, you gotta focus on the fundamentals.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.line: First thing's first: house-training. You can't go anywhere without nailing the house-training.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.line: That's what separates the amateurs from the professionals.

jokes.text: I'm gonna tell you the same thing I told Al Minza and his pyramid of dogs.
jokes.setup: Estelle is about to give Joey career advice
jokes.punchline: She references a client 'Al Minza and his pyramid of dogs' — an utterly surreal act that exists only in this throwaway line
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great throwaway line. 'Pyramid of dogs' is a perfectly absurd image — specific enough to seem real, bizarre enough to be hilarious. Estelle representing a dog-pyramid act tells you everything about her client roster and explains why Joey is stuck with two-line roles. The specificity of naming it ('Al Minza') elevates it above generic absurdism. Economy is outstanding — four words create a whole world.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, this book is like, totally about Rachel. Like, every single chapter is describing her life. It's like the author followed her around or something.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, that's a self-help book. It's written for everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, no, no. See, it says here 'Chapter 3: Why You Can't Find Love When You're Only Thinking About Yourself.' That is SO you right now.

jokes.text: Take any job you can get, and don't make on the floor.
jokes.setup: Estelle is delivering serious career advice to Joey
jokes.punchline: The advice ends with 'don't make on the floor' — advice appropriate for a dog, not an actor, revealing her dog-act clients have conditioned her advice-giving
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the pyramid-of-dogs setup. 'Don't make on the floor' works on multiple levels: it's the callback, it's the absurd extension of dog-training logic into agent advice, and it's a perfectly understated non-sequitur. The pairing of jokes 15 and 16 is this episode's second-strongest comedic sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You're so controlling! You plan every single moment of our time together.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I am not controlling. I'm organized. There's a difference. And frankly, if we don't plan ahead, we won't get good seats at the movie theater. Do you know what happens at 7 PM on a Friday? Everyone shows up. Everyone. The theater has a finite number of seats—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, here we go...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, listen. If we don't buy tickets online in advance, we'll end up in the third row, craning our necks at an angle that will cause permanent cervical damage. Is that what you want? Because that's how people end up in neck braces, Rachel.

jokes.text: Actually, it's the movie theater that has the timetable. It's so you don't miss the beginning.
jokes.setup: Monica accuses Ross of controlling everything according to his timetable (because of the wind book's influence)
jokes.punchline: Ross literally, pedantically explains that movie theaters have timetables for practical reasons — completely missing the emotional subtext
jokes.explanation: Perfect Ross moment — his inability to read the room and default to literal correctness is core to his character. The explanation 'so you don't miss the beginning' is magnificently oblivious. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I am woman, hear me roar!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, that's from like the '80s.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So? It's still empowering!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's also still really embarrassing.

jokes.text: You go, girl! / I can't pull that off, can I?
jokes.setup: Monica stands up for herself against Ross; Chandler instinctively cheers her on with 'You go, girl!'
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately recognizes he cannot deliver this phrase authentically and checks in with the audience
jokes.explanation: A near-meta moment that works beautifully. Chandler's instant self-awareness about his own performative use of slang is very on-brand. The two-beat structure (commitment, then immediate doubt) is well-timed and has strong quotability. Chandler-specific and relatable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm down with the kids. I'm hip, I'm cool, I'm with it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Who am I kidding? I just said 'with it.'

jokes.text: How do you expect me to grow if you won't let me blow?
jokes.setup: Monica is earnestly arguing about her wind being stolen, using the book's wind metaphor
jokes.punchline: The sentence accidentally becomes a double entendre that everyone in the room (and audience) catches
jokes.explanation: The double entendre is unintentional on Monica's part — she's entirely sincere. The long pause before Ross's careful 'You know I don't... have a problem with that' is what makes it land. The audience reaction would be huge. Quotability is extremely high. The structure of Monica not realizing what she said while Ross navigates it carefully is textbook sexual innuendo comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: How can I grow if you won't let me blow?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I... well... that's not... I mean, the thing is...

jokes.text: Ross's careful, elongated pause and response: 'You know I don't... have a problem with that.'
jokes.setup: Monica says 'How do you expect me to grow if you won't let me blow?'
jokes.punchline: Ross's pause, then carefully worded non-response, confirms he clocked the double entendre and is navigating it diplomatically
jokes.explanation: The pause IS the joke. Ross cannot say 'I don't have a problem with that' without it landing wrong, and his careful navigation of it is the peak of this sequence. The pause-then-qualifier structure is textbook comedy timing. This and joke 20 together constitute one of the episode's best sequences.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm not going to apologize.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I'm sorry! I apologized!

jokes.text: I'm sorry. / Mm, mm, mm. You're right. I don't have to apologize. Sorry. Damn it!
jokes.setup: Monica, empowered by the wind book, stops herself from apologizing — then apologizes again reflexively, then catches herself
jokes.punchline: She apologizes for apologizing, then curses at herself — the habit is too deep to break
jokes.explanation: The escalating self-correction is well-structured — three beats of increasing self-contradiction. 'Damn it!' as the final beat is the perfect button. This works as character comedy because Monica's people-pleasing instinct vs. her new-found empowerment is the conflict made physical.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, you're telling me you keep a book by your bed just to... what, check which way the wind is blowing?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's not silly, Ross. It helps me sleep.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, I'm not blaming the book. I'm blaming literacy. If you couldn't read, none of this would be happening.

jokes.text: This is why I don't date women who read.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Ross are baffled by the wind book's effect on Monica and Rachel
jokes.punchline: Chandler delivers this as his settled conclusion — an absurdly reductive takeaway
jokes.explanation: Tight Chandler one-liner. The absurdist overcorrection (don't date women who read) as a solution to a minor problem is very on-brand. Good economy and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh no... there's a second envelope.

jokes.text: It's my VISA bill. Envelope one of two.
jokes.setup: Joey opens some mail — the audience expects routine
jokes.punchline: 'Envelope one of two' signals the bill is so large it required multiple envelopes
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical setup. 'Envelope one of two' is the entire joke in four words — the implication of a bill so enormous it needed two envelopes is conveyed with perfect efficiency. Character-specific (Joey's financial irresponsibility is established) and well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How was I supposed to know what he was saying? He had this crazy accent!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, he was from New Jersey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Exactly!

jokes.text: My animals. The guy said they suited me. He spoke with an accent. I was confused.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks how Joey spent $3500 at Porcelain Safari
jokes.punchline: Joey's three-part explanation — the animals suited him, the salesman had an accent, he got confused — is the logic chain of someone who cannot resist a persuasive foreign accent
jokes.explanation: Three beats, perfectly paced. 'He spoke with an accent. I was confused.' is the payoff — it's the exact kind of logic Joey uses, and it tells you everything about his susceptibility and his earnestness. The third beat delivers the confession so matter-of-factly that it lands as both funny and somehow sympathetic. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, you're in debt. You need to stop buying things you don't need.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, I know. I'm cutting back.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really? Because I just saw a charge from 'The Wig Emporium.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That was for a role!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, you bought seventeen wigs. What role requires seventeen wigs?

jokes.text: You can start by driving a cab on Another World.
jokes.setup: Joey says he doesn't know what to do about his debt
jokes.punchline: Chandler pivots back to the audition — using Joey's own financial crisis as leverage
jokes.explanation: Functional callback that uses the financial revelation to reframe the audition debate. Works as plot-comedy but isn't particularly witty.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Your work is reprehensible and your modus operandi is unconscionable.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wow, Joey, you're using big words. Did you finally start reading that word-a-day toilet paper?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because you're only getting like three words a day out of it.

jokes.text: I don't need you getting judgmental and condescending and pedantic. / Toilet paper? / Yeah.
jokes.setup: Joey uses the word 'pedantic' in an argument with Chandler
jokes.punchline: Chandler's single-word 'Toilet paper?' confirms he knows exactly where Joey learned that word — and Joey confirms it without shame
jokes.explanation: This may be the episode's single most perfectly constructed comedic exchange. 'Toilet paper?' is two words that accomplish everything: it's the callback payoff, it acknowledges Joey's word source, it gently deflates Joey's attempted sophistication, and Chandler's one-word question contains equal parts fondness and disbelief. Joey's 'Yeah' — completely unashamed — is the button. The economy is near-perfect. This is what running-gag payoffs should look like.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How much do you owe?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I owe Chromantic $12,000.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Chromantic? What is that, a romantic restaurant for robots?

jokes.text: What I do know is you owe $2300 at 'Isn't It Chromantic?'
jokes.setup: Chandler is arguing with Joey about financial reality
jokes.punchline: He casually drops another absurd store name — 'Isn't It Chromantic?' — a chrome-furniture pun on 'Isn't It Romantic'
jokes.explanation: The pun store name is the joke — 'Isn't It Chromantic?' lands as a second absurd store in Joey's spending spree. The wordplay is clever and the casualness with which Chandler reads it is perfect. Continuing the running-store-name joke from Porcelain Safari.

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: This new goldfish is much feistier than the last one.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's because the last one was a cracker.

jokes.text: Chandler finds Eddie still in the apartment — dehydrating fruits and vegetables with an enthusiasm described as being 'a dehydrating maniac'
jokes.setup: Chandler comes home expecting Eddie to be gone; Eddie promised to leave
jokes.punchline: Eddie is not only still there, he has acquired a food dehydrator and is deeply invested in it
jokes.explanation: Eddie's spiral into food dehydration is a good absurdist character beat — the specificity of the hobby (not just 'still there' but ACTIVELY dehydrating) makes it funnier. 'I'm a dehydrating maniac!' is Eddie at his most gloriously unhinged.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What are you dehydrating?

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: Oh, just a kidney... I mean, a tomato.

jokes.text: Just some basic dehydrating of fruits and vegetables. Man alive, this thing's fantastic!
jokes.setup: Chandler returns home expecting Eddie to have moved out as promised
jokes.punchline: Eddie is still there, enthusiastically dehydrating produce, completely unfazed by having been told to leave
jokes.explanation: Eddie's enthusiastic domesticity while completely ignoring the eviction is funny. 'Man alive, this thing's fantastic!' about a dehydrator while Chandler stares in disbelief is a solid character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: You know, I understand what you're going through, Joey. I was an actor once too.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Really? What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: I died. On stage. During a production of Macbeth. They say I gave the most convincing death scene anyone had ever seen.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's... actually kind of amazing.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: Well, I was supposed to come back for the curtain call, but I had already made coffee plans.

jokes.text: I got us a new goldfish. He's feistier than the last one. / Maybe because the last one was made by Pepperidge Farm.
jokes.setup: Eddie cheerfully announces he got a new goldfish to replace the last one
jokes.punchline: Chandler reveals the previous 'goldfish' was actually a Pepperidge Farm goldfish cracker — Eddie thought a cookie was a living fish
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The setup is innocent — a new, feistier goldfish — and the punchline retroactively reveals Eddie's complete break from reality: he was keeping a goldfish cracker as a pet. The word 'feistier' makes it even better, because it means Eddie observed 'behavioral' differences between the cracker and the real fish. This tells you Eddie is not just eccentric but genuinely unmoored from consensus reality, and it does so with devastating economy. One of the episode's top-tier moments.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Out of the blue? Eddie, I've been dropping hints for months. I've been leaving eviction notices on your pillow. I hired a skywriter. There's a billboard on the highway!

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: Well, I didn't see any of that.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You didn't see the billboard?

jokes.text: Your last roommate's kidney? / That's a tomato.
jokes.setup: Eddie shows Chandler something he's been dehydrating, asking him to identify it
jokes.punchline: Chandler guesses it's a human organ; Eddie confirms it's just a tomato — but Chandler's guess reveals how far his paranoia about Eddie has gone
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Chandler's paranoia has reached the point where a shriveled tomato looks like a kidney, and the calm 'That's a tomato' response from Eddie who then puts it 'in the display' is equally disturbing. The 'display' of dehydrated items is a great background gag.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's pronounced 'Vin-chee,' not 'Vin-say.' Vin-chee.

dialogue.speaker: Casting Director
dialogue.line: It's actually 'Vin-say.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No no, I'm pretty sure it's 'Vin-chee.' Like Hawaii Five-O.

jokes.text: Oh. That sucks. I was buried in an avalanche. / What? / I used to be Brice on All My Children.
jokes.setup: Joey tells Gunther his Days of Our Lives character died falling down an elevator shaft; Gunther commiserates
jokes.punchline: Gunther reveals he too was a soap opera actor — killed in an avalanche — which nobody knew, including Joey
jokes.explanation: An excellent Gunther character moment. The reveal that the background Central Perk barista had his own soap opera career is a wonderful piece of world-building comedy. 'Brice on All My Children' feels entirely plausible for Gunther. The deadpan delivery of 'I was buried in an avalanche' as equivalent tragedy to Joey's situation is perfectly calibrated. High rewatch bonus — viewers notice Gunther differently after this.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I need to cross the budge to get to the other side.

dialogue.speaker: Casting Director
dialogue.line: It's 'bridge,' Joey. Bridge.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's what I said. Budge.

dialogue.speaker: Casting Director
dialogue.line: No, sweetheart. Bridge. Br-idge.

jokes.text: Why must everybody watch me sleep? There'll be no more watching me sleep! No more... watching!
jokes.setup: Chandler walks in to find Eddie apparently watching him again
jokes.punchline: Chandler's frustrated declaration that 'there'll be no more watching me sleep!' trails off as he loses the thread of his own sentence
jokes.explanation: Functional running gag callback. The 'No more watching!' trailing off is a nice bit of Chandler losing momentum mid-rant, but it doesn't add much to what the cold open already established.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So Monica, you're like the wind-keeper in that book, right? You're keeping everything in balance.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't know what that means, but okay.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, Chandler is like... he's the puppet.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: My husband is not a puppet!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A puppet that you control with love.

jokes.text: I got some great stuff to dehydrate. Grapes, apricots. I thought it'd be cool to see what happens with these water balloons.
jokes.setup: Chandler is trying to kick Eddie out; Eddie lists dehydrating items
jokes.punchline: Eddie adds 'water balloons' to his list of things to dehydrate, apparently not understanding what dehydrating is — or does
jokes.explanation: The water balloons addition is the joke — it's unclear if Eddie is being surreal or is genuinely confused about how dehydration works. Either way, it's a funny escalation of his obliviousness. The mundane list (grapes, apricots) makes the absurd final item land better.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh please, Monica, you won because you're built like a... like a... like a TREE! You have the reach of a sequoia!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That is not fair!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Fair?! You could practically high-five someone in New Jersey from here!

jokes.text: This is not out of the blue! This is smack-dab in the middle of the blue!
jokes.setup: Eddie says being asked to leave is 'kind of out of the blue'
jokes.punchline: Chandler inverts the idiom to insist the opposite — 'smack-dab in the middle of the blue'
jokes.explanation: A clever subversion of an idiom that also works as frustrated Chandler logic. 'Smack-dab in the middle of the blue' doesn't mean anything but it sounds like it does, which is the joke. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're like a rake in the wind.

jokes.text: If you think I'm leaving you alone with my fish, you're insane! / No help required, chico!
jokes.setup: Eddie is being asked to leave and someone offers to help him move his things
jokes.punchline: Eddie's primary concern in leaving is the safety of his fish — which we know is actually a real fish this time (not a cracker), making it a callback to his delusion, while 'chico' is an inexplicably random farewell
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat — Eddie's protectiveness of his fish is funny given the fish history. 'No help required, chico!' is random enough to get a mild laugh but not particularly crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, you might want to be careful with that. It's a 3-D Last Supper, and when you look at it from certain angles, it looks like... well, let's just say Jesus is very happy to see you.

jokes.text: That's 'fifty' bucks. Five-O dollars.
jokes.setup: Joey is reading his cab-driver audition lines from faxed (smudged) script pages; the cabbie says the fare is 'so bucks'
jokes.punchline: The director corrects him — it's 'fifty,' not 'so' — revealing Joey misread the smudged fax and didn't catch it
jokes.explanation: A decent visual-comedy-through-dialogue moment. Joey's commitment to the misread line and the director's politely bemused correction are the beats. The fax explanation is a necessary setup and slightly bogs it down.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey didn't get the audition? That's great!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Ross, that's not great. I didn't get the part.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, I know, but think about it — you didn't bomb the audition because you never went! It's perfect!

jokes.text: When I was on Days of Our Lives as Dr. Drake Ramoray, they'd send over the whole script on real paper.
jokes.setup: Joey is auditioning for a two-line cab driver role with a smudged fax script
jokes.punchline: Joey name-drops his former prestigious role mid-audition, reminding everyone (and himself) of his fallen status
jokes.explanation: Part of the episode's running 'I was Dr. Drake Ramoray' gag. The irony of telling your auditioners about your better days is cringe-comedy gold, and 'real paper' as the distinction is a perfect status-marker detail.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh hey, I picked up a little something today.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's a statue of an eagle. Only cost me twelve hundred bucks.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Twelve hundred dollars?!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I know, it was a little pricey, but I couldn't resist. It was right there at the checkout.

jokes.text: If you wanted to expand this scene, like have the cab crash... I could attend to the victims... because I have a background in medical acting.
jokes.setup: Joey is in a failed audition for a two-line cab driver role
jokes.punchline: Joey pitches improvising a medical emergency subplot so he can use his soap opera skills — 'medical acting' is his invented specialty
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy — Joey's attempt to leverage his neurosurgeon soap opera role as 'medical acting' experience for a two-line cab driver audition is perfectly in-character and deeply cringe-funny. 'Medical acting' as a self-coined sub-specialty is a great original coinage. The desperation is palpable and relatable.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's not behind Macy's. That's behind a Pottery Barn.

jokes.text: You were going for bridge there, weren't you?
jokes.setup: Joey reads 'budge' for 'bridge' in his audition
jokes.punchline: The director's exhausted, resigned question is the reaction beat — not even angry, just tired
jokes.explanation: The director's tone of quiet resignation is the joke. 'Weren't you?' softens it from accusation to a gentle, defeated confirmation request. Works as reaction comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: I'll call it a 'chick bowl'... no wait, a 'chip chick'... a 'chicip'!

jokes.text: I'll have a good day.
jokes.setup: The director dismisses Joey from the audition with 'okay, listen, thanks for coming in'
jokes.punchline: Joey says 'I'll have a good day' — a non-sequitur that functions as either mishearing 'have a good day' or a desperate, performative self-affirmation
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximally efficient. 'I'll have a good day' as a leaving statement is funny whether it's a misheard social formula or a deliberate declaration of intent after a humiliating audition. The ambiguity makes it richer. Joey's oblivious positivity vs. the obvious disaster of the audition is the comedic core.

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: Remember when we went to that baseball game and you caught that foul ball?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That never happened.

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: Sure it did! And then we went for hot dogs after!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

jokes.text: Question 28: 'Have you ever allowed a lightning-bearer to take your wind?' / I would have to say no. / And I would have to say, 'Pah, ha.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel are doing a self-assessment quiz from the wind book
jokes.punchline: Rachel confidently says no; Monica's laugh ('Pah, ha') indicates she disagrees completely
jokes.explanation: The wind-book quiz format is a good delivery vehicle for friends calling each other out. Monica's 'Pah, ha' is a funny phonetic laugh that signals she has receipts. Leads well into the puppet guy callback.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, sure, Eddie thinks he's a astronaut and he keeps trying to launch himself off the balcony, but... there's something kind of sweet about a guy who dreams that big.

jokes.text: Do you not remember the puppet guy? You totally let him wash his feet in the pool of your inner power. And his puppet too!
jokes.setup: Rachel claims she's never let a man take her wind
jokes.punchline: Monica invokes a specific ex — 'the puppet guy' — whose puppet ALSO washed its feet in Rachel's inner-power pool
jokes.explanation: 'And his puppet too!' is the escalation that makes this joke. The wind-book metaphor being applied to a man with a puppet — with the puppet receiving equal blame — is a brilliant absurdist layering. The specificity of 'his puppet too' suggests the puppet was somehow equally complicit in Rachel's wind-theft. Very funny and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: Okay, you know what? You're right. I don't live here. I never have. I've just been coming over every day, eating your food, using your shower, sleeping on your couch... but fine. I'll accept that I don't live here.

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: Actually, that's a relief. Do you know how much my rent would be?

jokes.text: Well, at least I didn't let some guy into the forest of my righteous truth on the first date!
jokes.setup: Rachel fires back at Monica's puppet-guy accusation
jokes.punchline: Rachel uses the book's metaphor ('forest of my righteous truth') as a euphemism for something physical happening on a first date
jokes.explanation: Good use of the wind-book metaphor as innuendo. The characters fighting in wind-book language while clearly talking about sexual history is funny. 'Forest of my righteous truth' is a memorably ridiculous euphemism.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, Eddie, I guess this is it. You know, I really hope you find what you're looking for out there. And hey, maybe one day you'll come back, nice and dried out.

jokes.text: Danny Arshack, ninth grade. / You know the bottle was pointing at me. / Only because you took up half the circle!
jokes.setup: Monica accuses Rachel of betraying a goddess (question 29); Rachel denies it; Monica invokes Danny Arshack from ninth grade
jokes.punchline: Rachel defends herself with the spin-the-bottle alibi; Monica destroys it with 'only because you took up half the circle'
jokes.explanation: 'Only because you took up half the circle' is a devastating physical insult wrapped in plausible-deniability about spin-the-bottle geometry. The specificity (ninth grade, Danny Arshack) grounds it, and the accusation that Rachel rigged the bottle by taking up more space is both petty and perfect. Gets a big laugh from the audience.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, what happened to the foosball?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Eddie dehydrated it into fruit.

jokes.text: Not when they find out you slept with Jason an hour after he broke up with Monica. / One hour? / You are such a leaf blower!
jokes.setup: Phoebe is being excluded from the goddess meetings for not taking sides; she deploys her ace
jokes.punchline: 'One hour?!' from Monica confirms this is news to her; Rachel's insult — 'leaf blower' — is using the wind-book metaphor as an insult, meaning Rachel 'blows away' others' wind
jokes.explanation: Three-beat joke that hits hard. Monica's 'One hour?' reveals she didn't know the detail and makes the revelation sting. 'You are such a leaf blower!' is a perfect creative insult that works both literally (wind metaphor) and as invented slang. Phoebe as the escalating chaos agent here is excellent character writing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, what's wrong with my ceramic dog?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Nothing, it's beautiful. Very lifelike. Except for one thing - it doesn't pee on the bathroom tiles.

jokes.text: Oh, hey, uh, be careful with that 3-D Last Supper. Judas is a little loose.
jokes.setup: The repo men are taking back all of Joey's purchased items
jokes.punchline: Among the items is a 3-D Last Supper, and Joey's concern is specifically that Judas figure is structurally compromised
jokes.explanation: A 3-D Last Supper is an inherently funny object to own, and the specificity that JUDAS is the loose figure adds a layer of accidental symbolism (the betrayer is coming undone). 'A little loose' as care instructions for a religious kitsch item is very funny. Joey's casual concern is perfect character delivery.

jokes.text: I could never do what you do. / Thanks. / You hold out for something bigger. I can't tell you how much respect I have for you not going to that stupid audition. / I went. / Great! How did it go? / I didn't get it. / Good for you! You're living the dream!
jokes.setup: Chandler comes to apologize and tell Joey he respects his artistic integrity in not going to the audition
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals he went, didn't get it; Chandler — committed to his supportive framing — can only keep escalating the positivity ('Good for you! You're living the dream!') to absurd heights
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured escalation. Chandler's speech builds up Joey for something that already went badly, and rather than retreating he doubles down with increasingly hollow positivity. 'You're living the dream!' as a response to 'I didn't get it' is the peak of ironic cheerleading. The structure is note-perfect.

jokes.text: How much for the, uh? How much to save the bird? / Twelve hundred. / Dollars? You spent $1200 on a plastic bird? / Uh, it was an impulse buy. Near the register.
jokes.setup: Repo men are taking Joey's ceramic animals; Ross tries to buy back the plastic parrot
jokes.punchline: The parrot costs $1200; Joey explains it was 'an impulse buy. Near the register.' — as if impulse-buy logic justifies $1200
jokes.explanation: 'Near the register' as justification for a $1200 purchase is perfect Joey logic — it reduces an absurd extravagance to a mundane retail impulse. Ross's 'Dollars?' is the right incredulous response. Good character comedy.

jokes.text: Do you have anything for around $200? / The dog. / I'll take it. My gift to you, man. / I really liked that bird, though. But the dog! Oh!
jokes.setup: Ross can't afford the $1200 parrot but wants to save something for Joey
jokes.punchline: He buys the ceramic dog instead, presents it as a gift — both of them know the parrot was cooler, but they convincingly pivot to enthusiasm for the dog
jokes.explanation: Sweet comedic beat about friendship making the best of a bad situation. The forced enthusiasm for the consolation dog after admitting they preferred the bird is relatable bromance humor. Not the sharpest joke but warmly landed.

jokes.text: You guys, this is not good. We have enough trouble with guys stealing our wind without taking it from each other.
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel are fighting; Phoebe brings peace offerings of cake
jokes.punchline: Phoebe uses the wind-book metaphor to mediate a fight — the absurd language applied to a real friendship conflict
jokes.explanation: Functional comedic use of the wind metaphor for emotional peacemaking. Phoebe is well-deployed as the sincere believer who uses the language without irony.

jokes.text: I don't ever want to suck your wind again.
jokes.setup: Monica is making up with Rachel and Phoebe using the wind metaphor
jokes.punchline: 'I don't ever want to suck your wind again' — another accidental double entendre that lands differently than intended
jokes.explanation: A milder version of the 'blow' double entendre from earlier. Works as a callback to that joke's structure but with less impact since the innuendo territory was already mined. 'Suck your wind' doesn't land quite as hard as 'won't let me blow.'

jokes.text: Okay, let me take these back. They'll take it out of my paycheck.
jokes.setup: The emotional reconciliation is complete; Phoebe ordered cakes they didn't ask for
jokes.punchline: The moment of warmth is undercut by the mundane reality that the cakes cost Phoebe money she can't afford
jokes.explanation: A nice comedic deflation of the emotional moment. Phoebe's practical poverty undercuts her grand gesture in a charming way. 'They'll take it out of my paycheck' is an endearingly sad button.

jokes.text: Ding-dong, the psycho's gone!
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey celebrate that Eddie has finally left
jokes.punchline: Chandler's victory cry is a Wizard of Oz reference reframed as 'Ding-dong, the PSYCHO's gone' — a twist on 'ding-dong the witch is dead'
jokes.explanation: A clean, economical pop culture subversion. The swap from 'witch' to 'psycho' is the only change needed and it's the right one. High quotability; this line would likely get a big audience response as a release valve after the Eddie storyline.

jokes.text: That guy is holding a human head! He's holding a human head!
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey are celebrating Eddie's departure; someone looks out the window
jokes.punchline: Eddie can be seen outside holding what appears to be a mannequin head — Chandler (and the audience) don't know this yet
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag that plays on Eddie's established creepiness. The doubled 'He's holding a human head!' (said twice for emphasis) is a classic sitcom alarm-beat. The reveal that it's a mannequin head is the payoff.

jokes.text: I tore it off a mannequin in the alley behind Macy's. / There is no alley behind Macy's. / So I got it in the junior miss department. Big diff.
jokes.setup: Eddie explains the mannequin head
jokes.punchline: When called out on the fictional alley, Eddie immediately revises to the junior miss department with 'Big diff' — the location shift is treated as a trivial detail, not the disturbing content of his story
jokes.explanation: 'Big diff' is a perfect Eddie line — he concedes the factual correction with zero embarrassment while completely missing that the real issue is tearing a head off a mannequin. His priorities are completely inverted and it's wonderfully in character. The casual slang ('Big diff') from someone carrying a mannequin head is surreally funny.

jokes.text: Yeah, you know, we'll put chips in it. We'll make it a chip chick.
jokes.setup: Eddie suggests the mannequin head as a cocktail-party conversation piece
jokes.punchline: 'Chip chick' — Eddie's plan to fill the severed mannequin head with chips and serve them at a party, naming the serving vessel
jokes.explanation: 'Chip chick' is an inspired coinage. Eddie naming a mannequin-head chip bowl 'chip chick' with complete confidence and domestic pride is peak Eddie-as-unhinged-but-earnest. The specificity and casualness of 'chip chick' make it absurdly funny and highly quotable. One of the episode's best individual lines.

jokes.text: We took a road trip to Las Vegas! / Oh, sweet Moses! / So on this road trip, uh, did you win any money? / Nah, I crapped out. But Mr. 21 here! He cleans up! $300! He buys me these new shoes. Sweet, huh?
jokes.setup: Chandler asks what happened yesterday — expecting Eddie to say he moved out
jokes.punchline: Eddie's memory of yesterday is an elaborate Las Vegas road trip with Chandler — a trip that definitely never happened
jokes.explanation: A great Eddie set piece — the Las Vegas road trip is elaborately detailed (crapped out, Mr. 21, $300, new shoes) which makes it funnier than a vague false memory. Chandler's 'Oh, sweet Moses!' is the right reaction. The shoes as physical evidence Eddie believes this happened is a nice touch. 'Sweet, huh?' with complete pride is perfect.

jokes.text: Is anyone else starting to really like him?
jokes.setup: Eddie has just described an elaborate fictional Las Vegas trip and departed with 'see you upstairs'
jokes.punchline: Joey — who has no reason to dislike Eddie — admits he's charmed by Eddie's enthusiasm and storytelling
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy — nine words that flip the entire emotional dynamic. After an episode of Eddie being terrifying, Joey's completely sincere 'Is anyone else starting to really like him?' is both a great character beat (Joey's unconditional enthusiasm for people) and a comedic release. The audience likely agrees, which is why it works. High quotability.

jokes.text: Chandler and Joey gaslight Eddie — pretending not to know him, having Joey pose as Chandler's 'new roommate'
jokes.setup: Chandler has tried every direct approach to remove Eddie; now he denies knowing him entirely
jokes.punchline: Eddie actually seems to accept this and wanders off confused — the scheme works because Eddie's grasp on reality is already tenuous
jokes.explanation: Good dark-comedy escalation — the solution to the problem is exploiting Eddie's genuine confusion about reality. Chandler's increasingly committed performance ('I already have a roommate. Hello.') is very funny. The scheme working is both satisfying and slightly troubling.

jokes.text: May I help you? / Why doesn't my key work, and what's my stuff doing downstairs? / I'm sorry. Have we met? / It's Eddie, you freak! Your roommate.
jokes.setup: Chandler's plan: he and Joey pretend not to know Eddie, having changed the locks and moved his stuff out
jokes.punchline: Chandler greets Eddie as a stranger; Eddie's exasperated 'It's Eddie, you freak!' hits differently because from Eddie's perspective this is incomprehensible
jokes.explanation: The gaslighting scheme is funny because it's so brazen and because Eddie's 'you freak' is genuinely warranted — Chandler IS being a freak by pretending not to know him. The irony of Eddie calling Chandler a freak after everything we've seen is strong. 'I'm sorry. Have we met?' is delivered with exactly the right amount of innocent confusion.

jokes.text: Well, I think we'd remember something like that. / I know I would. Ha, ha.
jokes.setup: Eddie insists he's been living there; Chandler and Joey double down on not knowing him
jokes.punchline: Joey's 'I know I would. Ha, ha.' — adding a chuckle as if the idea of him not remembering a roommate is genuinely absurd to him
jokes.explanation: Joey's 'Ha, ha' as punctuation to his own line is funny — he's playing a character (stranger who knows their roommate) and breaks into an almost theatrical chuckle. Works within the gaslighting sequence.

jokes.text: Okay, wow. Huh. I guess I got the wrong apartment. Look, I'm... I'm terribly sorry. / Hey, no problem. See you.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey are gaslighting Eddie into thinking he has the wrong apartment
jokes.punchline: Eddie — despite all evidence of his own existence as their roommate — accepts this and apologizes for the confusion, fully capitulating
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Eddie's grip on reality is so tenuous — established by the Las Vegas road trip and Pepperidge Farm goldfish — that he can be talked out of knowing where he lives. 'I guess I got the wrong apartment' from someone who has been living there is darkly funny. Chandler's breezy 'See you' as a goodbye to someone he's never met is the button.

jokes.text: Goodbye, you fruit-drying psychopath.
jokes.setup: Eddie leaves and the door closes; Chandler says his private farewell
jokes.punchline: 'Fruit-drying psychopath' — the specific detail of the dehydrator as Eddie's defining character trait in Chandler's mind
jokes.explanation: A satisfying, specific farewell that crystallizes the whole Eddie arc. Out of all Eddie's insanities, Chandler's farewell fixates on the fruit dehydrating — which is both mundane and emblematic of the whole bizarre situation. 'Fruit-drying psychopath' is an excellent compound noun. High quotability.

jokes.text: After Eddie leaves: 'Goodbye, you fruit-drying psychopath.'
jokes.setup: Eddie has finally left the apartment for good
jokes.punchline: 'Goodbye, you fruit-drying psychopath.' — Chandler's epitaph for Eddie combines the mundane (fruit-drying) with clinical (psychopath) for a perfectly Chandler farewell
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable lines. 'Fruit-drying psychopath' is a brilliant compound — it takes the most specific, mundane detail of Eddie's behavior and fuses it with a clinical diagnosis to create a perfect summation of his character. The callback to the dehydrating makes it feel earned. Chandler saying it to himself, alone, is also very him — he can't resist the epigram even when no one will hear it. Strong 8+ territory.

jokes.text: Just so you know, I'm not moving back in because I have to. I mean, I do have to, but... It's just that that place, it wasn't really... I mean, this is... / Welcome home, man.
jokes.setup: Joey is moving back in; he wants to maintain dignity while clearly needing to
jokes.punchline: 'I mean, I do have to, but...' — Joey immediately undercuts his own claim of choice with the admission that it's financially necessary, then trails into sentiment
jokes.explanation: A warm character beat with a comedic edge. The immediate self-correction ('I do have to') is the funny part; the rest is sentiment. 'Welcome home, man' is the perfect Chandler button — understated warmth.

jokes.text: What happened to the foosball? / It's a cantaloupe.
jokes.setup: The guys sit down for foosball; one of the balls has been replaced
jokes.punchline: A foosball has been replaced by a cantaloupe — Eddie's dehydrating hobby has apparently affected the foosball table
jokes.explanation: A beautiful tag joke. The cantaloupe in the foosball table is a perfect visual punchline that requires no setup — the audience immediately understands Eddie put fruit in everything. Economy is outstanding: two sentences, one exchange, complete payoff. This is a textbook example of an episode-closing tag that honors the running gag with maximum efficiency.

jokes.text: Are we gonna bring this out every time Ross comes over? / He paid a lot of money for it.
jokes.setup: The ceramic dog from Porcelain Safari is sitting out
jokes.punchline: Chandler confirms they will be displaying the dog indefinitely out of obligation to Ross's $200 purchase
jokes.explanation: A mild tag joke — the obligation to display a gift the recipient didn't want is relatable, but it's not particularly sharp. Functional episode-closer.

jokes.text: If you hated it so much, why'd you buy it in the first place? / Well, I had a whole ceramic-zoo thing going over there. But without the other ones, it looks tacky.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks why Joey bought the ceramic dog if he finds it tacky
jokes.punchline: Joey explains he had a 'ceramic-zoo thing going' — the full context being that without the rest of the repossessed collection, the lone dog looks tacky
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Joey's taste level is revealed: he was going for 'ceramic zoo' as an aesthetic, and it made sense in context. A single dog without the zoo is indeed tacky by that logic. Joey's interior design sensibility is unexpectedly coherent and that's the joke.

jokes.text: Is he housetrained or will he leave little bathroom tiles all over?
jokes.setup: The ceramic dog is being discussed; Ross is holding it
jokes.punchline: Chandler asks if it's housetrained — making a joke that ceramic tile dogs would leave ceramic tiles as waste
jokes.explanation: 'Little bathroom tiles' as the waste product of a ceramic dog is a genuinely clever logical extension — if a real dog leaves droppings, a ceramic dog would leave ceramic material. The wordplay is original and specific. Good closing joke for Chandler.

jokes.text: Stay. / Uh, stay! / Good fake dog.
jokes.setup: Ross is holding the ceramic dog
jokes.punchline: Ross gives the inanimate ceramic dog commands ('stay'), then compliments it — 'good fake dog' is the payoff
jokes.explanation: The episode's final joke — 'Good fake dog' is a perfect, economical button. Ross commanding a ceramic statue and then complimenting its obedience is gentle, warm absurdism. The pause between 'Stay.' and 'Uh, stay!' suggests he briefly forgot it wasn't real. Excellent economy — three words, total payoff.

tmdb_overview: Creeped out by his bizarre new roommate, Chandler demands he move out; Eddie agrees... but won't go. Joey has trouble coming to grips with the death of Dr. Drake Ramoray and is facing some exorbitant bills. And a new book on women's empowerment inspires the ladies to have a "goddess meeting."
insight: Eddie's presence generates 47 jokes in 22 minutes—nearly triple the show's baseline density.
